name: Monty Hall problem
seoDesc: Monty Hall problem: a free statistics calculator that walks you through 21 values, with the formula spelled out and a worked example.
summary: The Monty Hall problem calculator returns data from the 7 fields on the form. No sign-up, no page reload, and the relationship behind it is printed below. That makes it useful for an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Monty Hall problem calculator work?
sections.html:
The Monty Hall problem calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports data in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the strategy); then you type in how many games?.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as I want to play and I want to simulate. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as always keep the initial door and always change the door. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 3 options, such as door 1, door 2 and door 3. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Sure!”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as change and don't change. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Show me!”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.

6 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Monty Hall problem calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Data=(which door do you choose?)
Car is behind door number=rounded down, ((1 ÷ 100) × (which door do you choose?))
Open door number=rounded down, ((1 ÷ 10) × (which door do you choose?) − 10 × rounded down, ((1 ÷ 100) × (which door do you choose?)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Monty Hall problem calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Checking a result a piece of software produced

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Monty Hall problem calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns data. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Monty Hall problem calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for a few values, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (6 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Monty Hall problem calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
